extracted.intended_audience: psychology researchers, survey designers, and annotators assessing humor/joke quality
extracted.subtask_description: Use the Humor Styles Questionnaire (HSQ) framework to classify jokes and judge joke quality by style, adaptiveness, audience-appropriateness, and relational effects. Suitable for researchers, annotators, or moderators evaluating jokes across contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Affiliative Humor
rubrics_metrics.description: Sharing humor to amuse others; telling jokes or funny stories that bring people together; strengthens relationships; self-tolerant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this label when the joke's primary function is social bonding or in-group cohesion. Examples: observational jokes that invite shared laughter. Consider appropriateness for audience — affiliative humor is common in mainstream outlets (e.g., New Yorker) and forums aiming for inclusive laughs (e.g., some r/Jokes).

rubrics_metrics.name: Self-Enhancing Humor
rubrics_metrics.description: Maintaining a humorous outlook on life; coping with stress through perspective; finding humor in adversity; an internal coping mechanism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply when the joke reflects resilience or a positive, stress-buffering stance. This style indicates adaptive personal coping rather than aiming primarily to amuse others or attack someone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aggressive Humor
rubrics_metrics.description: Sarcasm, teasing, ridicule, derision used to manipulate or put others down; includes sexist or racist jokes; short-term pleasure at others' expense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Label jokes that demean, belittle, or target others (punching down). Note trade-offs: aggressive humor often 'wins laughs' but harms relationships and may be inappropriate for many audiences/platforms. Examples include ridicule, insults, or derogatory stereotypes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Self-Defeating Humor
rubrics_metrics.description: Excessively self-disparaging attempts to amuse others by putting oneself down; may hide underlying negative feelings and relate to depression.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use when the comedian or joke voice sacrifices self-respect to gain approval. Consider mental-health implications and maladaptiveness; may be socially bonding in the short term but signals underlying distress.

rubrics_metrics.name: Which humor style does this joke exemplify?
rubrics_metrics.description: Classify the joke according to the HSQ's four styles (affiliative, self-enhancing, aggressive, self-defeating).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determine primary style based on intent, content, and function. Note that the same joke could be affiliative or aggressive depending on context and audience — choose the label that best fits the observed intent/effect in situ.

rubrics_metrics.name: Is the style appropriate for the audience?
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate whether the identified humor style fits the norms, sensitivities, and expectations of the target audience or platform.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider platform examples (e.g., r/Jokes often tolerates more affiliative/aggressive banter; New Yorker favors affiliative/observational). Assess risks of offense or harm: aggressive humor may be inappropriate for mixed or vulnerable audiences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Does it strengthen or harm relationships?
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess the relational effect of the joke — whether it builds social bonds or damages them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Affiliative and some self-enhancing humor typically strengthen relationships; aggressive humor can harm relationships despite eliciting laughs; self-defeating humor may create short-term rapport but indicate personal harm. Use observed reactions and context to judge net effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Is the comedian using it adaptively or maladaptively?
rubrics_metrics.description: Judge whether the humor style is being used in a psychologically adaptive (beneficial) or maladaptive (harmful) way.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adaptive use: coping, bonding, resilience (affiliative, self-enhancing). Maladaptive use: harming others, masking distress, self-denigration (aggressive, self-defeating). Consider frequency, intent, and downstream effects (e.g., impact on mental health or relationships).

rubrics_metrics.name: Does the joke serve a coping or attacking function?
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine whether the primary function of the joke is to cope with adversity/internal states or to attack/manipulate others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Coping functions align with self-enhancing or self-defeating styles (internal processing, stress relief); attacking functions align with aggressive humor. Some affiliative jokes serve social cohesion rather than strictly coping or attacking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider function, context, and intent in quality assessment
rubrics_metrics.description: Quality assessment should consider the joke's function, the context and audience, and the comedian's intent because identical content can map to different styles depending on these factors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When rating joke quality, explicitly weigh intent (e.g., bonding vs. belittling), context (platform norms, audience makeup), and likely relational outcomes. Recognize trade-offs: a joke that elicits laughs (especially aggressive humor) may still be low-quality if it harms relationships or is inappropriate for the audience.
